Public Comment: The public is encouraged to address City Council on any matter listed on the agenda or on any other matter
within its jurisdiction subject to the rules of decorum described in Section 2.08.020 of the Norwalk Municipal Code. If you wish to
address City Council, please complete a speaker card and hand the card to the Sergeant at Arms. City Council will hear public
comment on items listed on the agenda during discussion of the matter and prior to a vote and on matters not listed on the agenda
during the Oral Communications period.

Pursuant to provisions of the Brown Act, no action may be taken on a matter unless it is listed on the agenda, or unless certain
emergency or special circumstances exist. The City Council may direct staff to investigate and/or schedule certain matters for
consideration at a future City Council meeting.

Please adhere to the following procedures when addressing the City Council: Comments should be limited to 3 minutes or less
and
directed to the City Council as a whole and not directed to individual Councilmembers.

Americans with Disabilities Act: In compliance with the ADA, if you need special assistance to participate in a City meeting or
other services offered by this City, please contact the City Clerk’s department, (562) 929-5720. Assisted listening devices are
available at this meeting. Ask the City Clerk if you desire to use this device. Upon request, the agenda and documents in the
agenda packet can be made available in appropriate alternative formats to persons with a disability. Notification of at least 48
hours prior to the meeting or time when services are needed will assist the City staff in assuring that reasonable arrangements
can be made to provide accessibility to the meeting or service.

Note: Any writings and/or documents provided to a majority of the City Council regarding any item on this agenda after it has
been posted will also be made available for public inspection. Writings and/or documents are available for inspection in the City
Clerk’s Department, during regular business hours, 8:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m., Monday – Thursday and 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., every
other Friday; telephone (562) 929-5720. You may also contact the City Clerk via e-mail at recordsrequests@norwalkca.gov.

AWARD OF CONTRACT – CONTINUED ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT CONSULTING
SERVICES

Alex Hamilton, Interim Director of Community Development, provided a report alongside
Ken K. Hira, President, and Fernando Sanchez, Vice President, both from Kosmont
Companies. City Council discussion ensued with Councilmember Rios expressing
concern with the role Kosmont plays in helping the City of Norwalk’s economic
development; requested that Kosmont be present at City Council Meetings for quarterly
report discussions. Councilmember Ramirez thanked Kosmont and expressed concern
with marketing properties that are not owned by the City; discussed agreement services
also being provided to the Enhanced Infrastructure Financing District Public Financing
Authority (EIDF). Vice Mayor Perez thanked Kosmont and mentioned the valuable
resources they provide. At the conclusion of discussion, Vice Mayor Perez moved and
Councilmember Valencia seconded to award a contract to Kosmont Companies for
continued economic development consulting services for a three-year term in an amount
not to exceed $100,000 each year; and authorized the City Manager to execute an
agreement and any amendments provided there is funding in the budget, and it is within
the City Manager’s signing authority, on behalf of the City, in a form approved by the City
Attorney. MOTION CARRIED BY THE FOLLOWING ROLL CALL VOTE:

HEART OF NORWALK SPECIFIC PLAN UPDATE

Carlos Rojas, Senior Planner, alongside Phil Burns, Principal with the Arroyo Group,
provided a report on the Heart of Norwalk Draft Specific Plan and provided feedback.
Addressing City Council on this item were Lisa Vernola Salas, Brian Tindall, and Daniel
Moreno. City Council discussion ensued with Councilmember Ramirez expressing
concern about the feasibility of the proposed plan. Vice Mayor Perez requested outreach
to business owners, a realistic approach be presented at the August meeting, and
recommended staff review that could potentially limit future developments.
Councilmember Rios expressed concern with the feasibility of the proposed plan. Mayor
Ayala requested a historical timeline of all the communication engagements made
regarding the Heart of Norwalk. The report was received and filed.

Background:

The City Council retained the law firm of Alvarez-Glasman & Colvin (“AGC”) pursuant to
agreement for City Attorney Services with AGC (“Agreement”) in 2019 with Arnold M. Alvarez-
Glasman appointed and serving as City Attorney for the City of Norwalk. Aside from providing

services in the region. Additionally, said agreement allowed for an automatic rate adjustment
annually consistent with the adjustment to the Consumer Price Index (CPI). AGC has requested
only one adjustment in their nearly six years of serving as City Attorney which was approved in
2022.

Recently a request was made by AGC to adjust their rates to make the retainer and hourly rates
comparable with CPI adjustments allowed and consistent with other rates being charged by other
law firms providing city attorney legal services. AGC is requesting the following rate adjustments
to the monthly retainer in the amount of $18,750 for the first 75 hours of basic legal services at
the rate of $250 per hour and $275 per hour for excess legal services provided each
month. Special legal services (real estate, litigation, complex contract matters and
labor/personnel matters) would be set at $295.00 for Partners, $290 for Senior Associates,
$285.00 for Associates. These Retainer and Special Service rates are still substantially below
hourly rates charged to the City by outside special counsel and by law firms providing similar
services in neighboring cities as outlined in the attached correspondence.

Finally, the Agreement needs to be amended to define the Term of the AGC’s services to be
continuous until terminated. This approach is identical to the term provided to the City’s previous
law firm and consistent with the approach followed by most cities in the region.

By approving the attached First Amendment, the rates for City Attorney legal services with
Alvarez-Glasman & Colvin would be adjusted accordingly effective July 1, 2025. With the

SUBJECT: RESOLUTION NO. 25-30 - SUPPORT OF AN APPLICATION FOR LAND AND
  WATER CONSERVATION FUND GRANTS

Background:

Land and Water Conservation Fund (LWCF) grants provide funding for the acquisition or development of
land to create new outdoor recreation opportunities for the health and wellness of Californians. Since
1965, over one thousand parks throughout California have been created or improved with LWCF
assistance. The LWCF is a current competitive grant program for both local and state agencies under the
California Department of Parks and Recreation (DPR).

The LWCF provides funding for acquisition projects or development projects. Examples of
acquisitions may include the creation of a new park or the expansion of an existing park. Examples of
development may include those for outdoor recreation, and may include, but not be limited to, features
such as athletic courts, fields, dog parks, picnic areas, outdoor trails, and aquatic features. The
deadline for the application is August 5, 2025. The local agency maximum grant request is $6 million with
a match requirement of 50%.

The Recreation and Park Services Department will be applying for the LWCF grant program. The
application process requires an approved resolution from the City of Norwalk City Council. If awarded,
grant funds will go towards the Norwalk Park expansion project.

Background:

On August 6, 2024, City Council adopted Urgency Ordinance No. 24-1752U, a 45-day
moratorium to establish, implement, or operate (temporarily or permanently) convenience
stores (liquor stores), discount stores, personal use – laundromat, vehicle/automobile washing,
payday loan establishments, emergency shelters, single-room occupancy, supportive housing,
and transitional housing city-wide (“Moratorium”). Urgency Ordinance No. 24-1752U included a
waiver process for those requesting to establish the listed uses during the Moratorium.

After a 10-day report was received and filed by City Council on September 3, 2024, the
Moratorium was extended on September 17, 2024 under Urgency Ordinance No. 24-1753U (see
Attachment 1) for an additional 10 months and 15 days and is set to expire on August 5, 2025,
unless extended for an additional year by City Council pursuant to Government Code Section
65858(a).

Prior to City Council consideration of the second (and final) extension of the Moratorium, City
Council is required to issue a “10-day report”, which describes the measures taken to alleviate
the condition in which led to the adoption of Urgency Ordinance No. 24-1753U. Per Government
Code Section 65858(d), this action is required before any extension of an urgency ordinance.

Convenience stores (liquor stores), discount stores, personal use – laundromat,
vehicle/automobile washing, and payday loan establishments - Prior to the adoption of the
Moratorium, the establishment and operation of the aforementioned uses was a concern by
virtue of their operational characteristics. Staff has researched to determine if these uses may
have detrimental effects (i.e., maintenance, proliferation, security issues, loitering, noise, and
economic impacts) on the community. To date, staff has completed the following research:

1. Reviewed City business license records to quantify the number of each type of use operating
within the City to determine if there is a saturation of these uses;
2. Initiated studies of land use tables for surrounding cities for the same or similar uses to
determine if the uses are permitted by right, not permitted or permitted with a discretionary review
(such as a conditional use permit);
3. Studied surrounding cities’ development and operational standards for aforementioned uses;
and
4. Researched various sources (i.e., American Planning Association, Urban Land Institute),
publications and articles on the aforementioned uses.

Due to the various uses and issues studied, additional time is needed for the next steps, which
would be for staff to initiate a zoning code text amendment(s) that will clarify definitions of the
aforementioned uses and provide additional regulations which may include (but are not limited
to) standards for the following:
  1. Discretionary review requirements;
  2. Distance requirements (i.e., from other uses, from sensitive uses, etc.);
  3. Development standards (i.e., minimum lot size, standards for new developments to
  minimize the need for these uses (i.e., in-unit laundry hookups for new residential units));
  and
  4. Operational standards (i.e., property maintenance and security).

Emergency shelters, single-room occupancy, supportive housing, and transitional housing
(“housing uses”) – During the COVID-19 pandemic, the County of Los Angeles (“County”)
operated Project RoomKey at 12500 Firestone Boulevard without input from the community.
Upon closure of Project RoomKey in 2021, individuals who were housed were not provided with
an exit plan.

Following the closure of Project RoomKey, the County received a $52 million encampment
resolution grant, which included Norwalk. Due to the experience of the Project RoomKey in the
City, Norwalk officials requested that Persons Experiencing Homelessness (“PEH”) not be
located at 12500 Firestone Boulevard and alternative sites were provided.

Despite the request, the County selected 12500 Firestone Boulevard for a two-year transitional
housing program without consideration of City and community interests and an exit plan at the
conclusion of the housing program. Given the poor performance of Project RoomKey, City
Council directed staff to draft an Urgency Ordinance pursuant to Government Code Section
65858. Since the adoption of the Moratorium, the City and the County have had productive

Following this action, the State of California filed a lawsuit against the City on the grounds of

Background:

The Los Angeles County Aging and Disabilities Department (ADD) runs the Elderly Nutrition
Program (ENP), which provides funding through grants and subawards for the congregate and
home delivered meal program, also known as the Senior Nutrition Program, for the senior citizen
population of the City. In Fiscal Year 2019/20 the City and ADD mutually agreed to collaborate
though a direct agreement to achieve the City’s objective of effectively serving the senior
community. This agreement allows the City to provide meals to both our congregate meal sites
and to our 225 participants of home delivered meal program daily, Monday through Friday.
Totaling over 121,000 meals for the fiscal year.

In 2023, the City partnered with Trio Community Meals, LLC (TCM), for catering services. They
are one of the several caterers the LA County permits the City to use. The cost for each individual
meal is competitive with most LA County approved caterers. TCM are quick to respond to any
questions or adjustments requested by staff. The quality of the meals has dramatically increased
attendance for congregate meals and is regularly acknowledged by the patrons. It is in the best
interest of the Senior Nutrition Program to renew TCM’s services for Fiscal Year 2025/26.

Fiscal Impact:

Operating funds for the Senior Nutrition Program are provided by the Los Angeles County Aging
and Disabilities Department Grant, Elderly Nutrition Program 252606, and are included in the
Fiscal Year 2025/26 budget.

Background:

The City of Norwalk, in partnership with the Los Angeles County Aging and Disabilities
Department, administers the Supportive Services Program (SSP) to benefit senior residents in
the community. This grant enables the Norwalk Senior Center to deliver essential services that
support and sustain independent living for older adults, avoiding premature, or inappropriate,
institutionalization.

These funds are specifically allocated to provide homemaking, personal care, in-home respite,
and case management services to Norwalk seniors. The services are provided by in-home
workers who are contracted with the City. The SSP serves approximately 50 – 55 Norwalk
seniors per fiscal year.

Fiscal Impact:

The proposed amendment with the Los Angeles County Aging and Disabilities Department is in
the amount not to exceed $78,202. Allowing the Norwalk Senior Center to provide Case
Management, Personal Care, Homemakers, In-Home Respite Care, and Registry Services.
